traditions/episcopal-church-usa/summary: The first autonomous Anglican province outside the British Isles, organised after the American Revolution with bishops consecrated in Scotland (Seabury, 1784) and England (1787) and a constitution and Prayer Book adopted in Philadelphia (1789). Historically influential far beyond its size, it ordained women priests from 1976, consecrated a partnered gay bishop (2003) and authorised same-sex marriage rites (2015), decisions that strained relations within the Anglican Communion and contributed to the formation of ACNA.
traditions/episcopal-church-usa/distinct: Democratic synodical government with lay deputies (General Convention)
Dioceses in 17 countries, including Latin America and Taiwan
Progressive positions on women's ordination and sexuality
traditions/episcopal-church-usa/profile/: Scripture as containing all things necessary to salvation, read with the creeds, the early Fathers and reason; the Thirty-Nine Articles, Book of Common Prayer and Ordinal as historic formularies.
Justification by grace through faith in Christ, with an emphasis on growth in holiness through the Church's common prayer and sacraments.
Two dominical sacraments (baptism and Eucharist) and five other 'commonly called sacraments'; views of Eucharistic presence range from Reformed to Anglo-Catholic.
The creedal hope of Christ's return, resurrection and judgement; prayer for the departed accepted in some traditions of the church.
General Convention with a House of Bishops and a House of Deputies (clergy and laity); a Presiding Bishop.
Book of Common Prayer (1979) and The Hymnal 1982.
The 66-book canon; the Apocrypha read 'for example of life' but not to establish doctrine (Article VI).
traditions/episcopal-church-usa/status: Active; c. 1.5 million baptised members in the early 2020s, declining.
traditions/church-of-nigeria/summary: One of the largest provinces of the Anglican Communion, rooted in the Church Missionary Society missions at Badagry and Abeokuta (1840s) and the ministry of Samuel Ajayi Crowther, consecrated in 1864 as the first African Anglican bishop. A separate province since 1979, it grew rapidly in the 1990s and became a leading voice of theologically conservative global Anglicanism through GAFCON.
traditions/church-of-nigeria/distinctive: Very rapid growth and many new dioceses
Ministry in contexts of Christian–Muslim tension in the north

traditions/church-of-nigeria/profile/can: The 66-book canon; the Apocrypha read 'for example of life' but not to establish doctrine (Article VI).
traditions/church-of-nigeria/status: Active; it claims around 18 million members, a figure that is difficult to verify.
traditions/anglican-church-of-kenya/summ: A province of the Anglican Communion rooted in the Church Missionary Society mission begun by Johann Ludwig Krapf at Mombasa in 1844 and deeply shaped by the East African Revival. It became the Church of the Province of Kenya in 1970 and took its present name in 1998. Its leaders have played prominent roles in national public life and in the GAFCON movement.

Ordination of women priests (since 1983 in some dioceses)

traditions/church-of-uganda/summary: The Anglican church of Uganda, rooted in the CMS mission at the court of Buganda (1877) and in the witness of the Uganda Martyrs (1885–87). Its piety was transformed by the East African Revival from the 1930s. It became a province in 1961; Archbishop Janani Luwum was murdered in 1977 after protesting abuses under Idi Amin.
traditions/church-of-uganda/distinctives: Strong presence in education and health care
Conservative position on sexuality and leadership in GAFCON

traditions/anglican-church-in-north-amer: A theologically conservative Anglican church formed in 2009 by dioceses and congregations that left the Episcopal Church and the Anglican Church of Canada, together with older bodies such as the Reformed Episcopal Church (1873). It regards itself as authentically Anglican and is recognised by the GAFCON primates, but it is not a member of the Anglican Communion's formal instruments. It includes evangelical, charismatic and Anglo-Catholic streams, and its dioceses differ on the ordination of women as priests.
